gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the XGIMI Horizon 20 measured only about 1,664 ANSI lumens in its normal Standard mode (Laurent Willen) and reached about 3,020 only in High Power mode. That is roughly 36% below the Nebula X1's 2,588 lumens in Standard (ProjectorCentral) and only about 17% above the Cosmos 4K SE's 1,426 (ProjectorCentral).
standout_why: Pages I opened: Wirecutter (cited, updated 2026-10-05) has Mars 3 figures (over 800 lm on a 100-inch screen, about 2 h at 100%, 4 h 45 min in eco at 20% brightness) but no X1 numbers, no Cosmos 4K SE and no Horizon 20 (it covers only the Horizon S Max, with no figures). ProjectorCentral's X1 review (in the results but not cited) has the X1 lumens table. GeekChamp (not cited, 2026-10-31) uses only maker ratings and says so. Pages I could not read: three RTINGS pages (cited) returned only site navigation, What Hi-Fi returned only its title, and Yahoo and Forbes returned 403. The RTINGS X1 review probably lists a measured X1 brightness, so the X1 figure alone may not stand out. No page I could read gives a measured Horizon 20 or Cosmos 4K SE brightness, and none gives the Mars 3's brightness in Eco power mode.
decides: This supports the X1 as the bright pick for a plugged-in backyard. ChatGPT's fourth card sells the $1,559 Horizon 20 as 'another strong bright-picture choice' at 3,200 ISO lumens. In its everyday picture modes it measured about 1,664 lm, against 2,588 for the X1. On a 120-inch screen with 1.0 gain that is about 39 fL versus 61 fL, which is closer to the cheaper Cosmos 4K SE (about 33 fL) than to the X1. For the battery pick, the Mars 3's longer runtime costs a lot of brightness: ProjectorCentral measured 959 lm at Standard power, falling to 442 lm in Eco power, and Wirecutter got about 2 h at 100%.
